t: as we have explained. Above 2:3, 2:9, 11:11.
as it is said, "whether he has seen or known". Hence he must see the act with his own eyes, or the litigant must admit it before him, so that he has complete knowledge of the matter.

and there is no testimony that stands on seeing or knowing except monetary testimony. But testimony in capital cases stands only on seeing alone, for Scripture decreed that capital cases are not judged on the admission of the litigant (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:6).

therefore they warn even witnesses in monetary cases. Since even in monetary cases one who heard from others may not testify, they put fear into them so that they testify only to what they themselves saw (Lechem Mishneh).
in front of everyone. In order to shame them so that they will not give false testimony (Radbaz).
if he said, "He told me, 'I owe him'". Since he said this by way of narration, it has no force as an admission (Peirush HaMishnayot, Sanhedrin 3:6).
"So-and-so told me that he owes him". He testifies that a certain person told him that another person owes his fellow, and this is testimony of one witness from another witness (hearsay).
"He admitted it to him in our presence". The defendant admitted to the plaintiff before the witnesses.
their statements are found to be consistent. Without contradiction between them.
they deliberate on the matter. And they decide the case on the basis of their testimony.
one who hides witnesses for his fellow. He concealed witnesses nearby.
but I fear that you will overpower me in court tomorrow. And I do not now have money to pay you.
this is not testimony. Since he did not know about the witnesses near him, he can claim that he was joking with him and did not mean his words seriously at all (see Hilchot To'ein VeNitan 6:7).
and he said it by way of admission. And not in the course of conversation (see Hilchot To'ein VeNitan 7:1).
or he said, "You are my witnesses," or "Be witnesses against me". For then in any case it is clear that he intends that they testify to his words.
whether the borrower said. That he owes the lender money.

or the lender said and the borrower was silent, as one who believes his words. That the lender said to the borrower in the presence of the witnesses that the latter owes him money, and the borrower was silent as a sign of agreement with his words.
they made a kinyan from his hand. They performed a kinyan sudar (acquisition by handing over an article) to give force to the statements (see Hilchot Mekhirah 5:5 and the commentary there).

exempt from human law. Even when he admitted that he hired them to testify falsely, he is not held liable in court, for there is no agency for a transgression, and the transgression is attributed to the agent and not to the sender.

but liable by the laws of Heaven. Morally he is responsible for what was done and ought to pay (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 2:19 and the Pesakim VeShitot there). This is where his fellow and the witnesses deny that they testified falsely, or admit it but for some reason payment cannot be collected from them (Sema, sec. 32, subsec. 3).
who suppressed his testimony and did not testify. He knows testimony in favor of his fellow and is unwilling to testify for him.
and there is a positive commandment to do to him as he intended to do through his testimony. As it is said: "Then you shall do to him as he had plotted to do to his brother" (Deuteronomy 19:19).
like other people liable to lashes, his strength is assessed. They assess how many lashes he can be given without dying (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 17:1).

they divide the money among themselves. Unlike a death or lashes penalty, where each of the witnesses is punished separately as he plotted, when they testified to make him liable for a certain sum of money, the payment is divided among them, so that the one they testified against ends up receiving the amount they wanted him to lose.

and they do not receive lashes in place of payment. For one does not receive lashes for a prohibition that can be remedied by payment (ibid. 18:2; Peirush HaMishnayot, Makkot 1:2; and see below 20:8-9, that a conspiring witness who cannot be done to as he plotted receives lashes).
there is no testimony here. The testimony is void.
contradiction of the testimony itself. It challenges the facts stated in the testimony.
it comes from the totality of its words. It can be understood from it.
and refutation of the witnesses themselves. It challenges the very presence of the witnesses at the event they testified about.
since the witnesses who refuted them did not pay any attention to the testimony itself. Rather, they testified about the witnesses.

they do not require forewarning. Unlike others liable to death or lashes, who are not punished if they were not forewarned before the transgression (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:1-2, 16:4), conspiring witnesses are punished without having been forewarned in advance (for the reason, see below 20:4).

who were contradicted and afterwards refuted. That first witnesses came and testified against them that the facts they testified about are untrue, and afterwards other witnesses came and testified against them that they were not present at that event at all.
these are put to death, etc.. Even though one might have said that once the testimony was contradicted there is no further room to refute it.
because contradiction is the beginning of refutation. And accordingly the refutation is regarded as a continuation of the contradiction.

witnesses are refuted only in their presence. Since the refutation concerns the witnesses themselves, and as they are the litigants, testimony against them is accepted only in their presence (Kesef Mishneh; and see above 3:11).
and witnesses are contradicted not in their presence. Since the contradiction concerns the testimony, and the witnesses are not a party to the matter.
and witnesses who were refuted not in their presence have been contradicted. Since challenging the witnesses' presence at the event includes also challenging the testimony.
even if the one said to be killed came on his own feet. Even if the one about whom they testified that he was murdered appeared alive before us, and it became entirely clear that the witnesses lied.
they do not receive lashes. Even though there are cases in which false witnesses are given lashes, when the law of refutation is not carried out on them (see below 20:8-9).

because it is a prohibition given as a warning of a court-imposed death penalty, etc.. Had the witnesses been refuted in a capital case, they would be liable to death by the court. And for any prohibition that carries a warning of a court-imposed death penalty, lashes are not given even when the death penalty is not carried out (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
they give them rebellion lashes as they see fit. For the court has authority to strike, as it sees fit, even one who is not liable to lashes by Torah law (ibid. 24:4).
it is a fine. And not compensation for monetary loss.

and therefore they do not pay on their own admission. On the basis of their admission, since it is a rule that one becomes liable for a fine only on the testimony of witnesses, and one who admits to a fine is exempt (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 2:8).

or if they said, "We testified against so-and-so about such-and-such, and we were refuted". They admitted that they were refuted in court (but did not admit that their sentence was finalized and they were obligated to pay).

for this is an admission of money whose payment has been adjudged. For once the court has obligated them to pay the fine, an ordinary monetary debt applies to them to pay it, and one who admits a debt must pay it.
and if one of them said, "I will pay my share". Even if only one of the witnesses whom the court obligated to pay admitted, he pays his proportionate share of the fine as the court obligated him.
the Birah. A large building.
they are not refuted. For there is not necessarily a contradiction between the testimonies.
a very light kar. A fast camel.
and they shortened the road with it. They crossed the road quickly, as if the road had become shorter for them.
even if the later ones testified that he killed him several days earlier. And they moved his liability earlier than the first ones did.

the killer is put to death, and his first witnesses are put to death, etc.. The killer is executed on the basis of the second group of witnesses, who testified that he killed the person, and the first witnesses are executed because they were refuted by them.
for at the time they testified that he killed him, his sentence of death had not yet been finalized. And it turns out that they plotted to kill a living person.

or his sentence was finalized on Monday. Even if they testified that his sentence was finalized after the time the first witnesses testified about (for example, the first say that his sentence was finalized on Sunday and the later ones say it was on Monday), nevertheless even the later ones agree that his death sentence was finalized before the first witnesses came to testify about it in court (for example, they came to testify on Tuesday).
for in any case, at the time they testified against him, his sentence of execution had already been finalized. And it turns out that they plotted to kill a person who is already considered dead.

the document is valid and the witnesses are valid, for it is possible that they postdated it and wrote it. And a document whose written date is later than the time it was actually written is valid (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 23:2).
and when they were in Jerusalem on the first of Adar they wrote this document there, etc.. And so there is no contradiction between the testimonies.

or witnesses who saw this document with their signatures on it on such-and-such a day. They did not see the witnesses sign the document, but they testify that on a certain day they saw the document signed.

they are disqualified retroactively from the day it became known that they signed the document. The disqualification of the witnesses applies retroactively from that day, and all the testimonies these witnesses have given since then are invalidated.
it is as if their testimony had been examined in court at the time of signing. As explained above 3:6, and so they are disqualified already from the time of signing.
fit for testimony. Qualified to testify.
after the judgment was finalized. Only after the court obligated the litigant on the basis of their testimony.
and one of them is found to be a relative or disqualified. And accordingly his testimony is void.

they are not punished, even though they were refuted and disqualified from all testimony in the Torah. For there is no connection between their disqualification from testifying because they testified falsely and the special punishment of "as he plotted."
they are not put to death by logical inference. Even though there would be room to execute them by a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument.
and this is from tradition. This law was learned through the tradition of the Sages.

but if the one they testified against received lashes, they receive lashes, etc.. For the teaching "as he plotted to do," meaning he had not yet done it, refers specifically to a case where they plotted to put their brother to death, and not where they plotted to make him liable to lashes or money (Radbaz, based on Mishnah Makkot 1:6).
and each of them testified after his fellow within the time of a statement. With only a very brief pause between them, as explained below.
they are not punished until all of them are refuted. Since all of them are considered one group.
and it is the time of a student's greeting to the teacher. The time to say the words "Peace upon you, my teacher" (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17).
and the two who were refuted are punished. Even though the other two were not refuted.

because they are one group. Since they came to testify together, they are considered one group regarding the voiding of testimony, so that if part of it is void, all of it is void (Radbaz, Kesef Mishneh, and as above 5:3-5).

and conspiring witnesses cannot act in error, because there is no act in them. There is no law of error for one who performed no act, as it is said: "You shall have one law for him who acts in error" (see Hilchot Shegagot 1:2). And conspiring witnesses performed no act, but testified by speech alone (Radbaz; and see the commentators who explained the matter itself in other ways).

therefore they do not require forewarning. In order to punish them, since forewarning is meant to distinguish between inadvertent and deliberate transgression (Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:2), and that does not apply here (and see Peirush HaMishnayot, Sanhedrin 11:4 and Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 33a, for other reasons why they do not need forewarning).
as we have explained. Above 18:4.
just as two refute a hundred if the hundred testified as one group. As explained above 18:3.
and those two stood up and refuted this second group too. That they also testified about the witnesses of the second group, that at that time they were with them in another place.
and it refuted the second group. They testified about them that at that time they were with them in another place.
the second group is put to death. For they plotted to kill the first group.
and Reuven. He too is put to death, for it became clear that the first group, which testified that Reuven killed Shimon, was valid.
a treifah person. A person with a severe defect who will die within a short time and has no cure, and who is considered dead to some extent.
that even if they killed him with their own hands they are not put to death because he is a treifah. As explained in Hilchot Rotze'ach 2:8.

witnesses who were treifah and testified about a matter for which one is liable to a court-imposed death penalty. This speaks of a case where the judges did not know that they were treifah and accepted their testimony, and only afterwards their condition became clear (Arukh HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 38:16).

for if their refuters are refuted, their refuters are not put to death because they refuted only a treifah. And since it is impossible to punish them if they are refuted, their testimony is not accepted, for testimony that you cannot refute is not considered testimony in capital cases (see Hilchot Rotze'ach 2:9).
these receive lashes. For the Sages received a tradition that conspiring witnesses who cannot be punished as they plotted to do receive lashes, as explained in the next halakhah.
and likewise if they testified about a person that he killed inadvertently. The law of one who kills inadvertently is that he is exiled to a city of refuge (Hilchot Rotze'ach 5:1).
and they are not exiled. For in this matter they are not punished with what they plotted to do.
and they do not pay the ransom. Even though the owner of an ox that was forewarned and killed a person pays ransom (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 10:2), they are not punished with what they plotted.
who was sold as a Hebrew slave. They testified about him that he stole and that the court sold him as a slave because he had no means to repay the theft (see Hilchot Genevah 3:11).
and these four matters are from tradition. A tradition of the Sages in the Oral Torah, that in these matters they receive lashes and are not punished in another way.

so the Sages received, etc.. From the verse "and they shall acquit the innocent and condemn the guilty. And if the guilty man deserves to be beaten..." (Deuteronomy 25:1-2), they derived that witnesses who initially wished to convict an innocent person and in the end were refuted, so that the innocent defendant was acquitted and the conspiring witnesses were condemned as wicked, receive lashes even though they did not plot to make him liable to lashes (see Babylonian Talmud, Makkot 2b).
but if they testified against him that he ate meat in milk or wore shatnez, these receive lashes. Like other conspiring witnesses, since they plotted to have him flogged.
and Reuven's sentence was finalized to strangulation, and the adulteress's to burning. As explained in Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 3:3.

these are strangled and not burned. Although one liable to two death penalties is judged by the more severe one, and burning is more severe than strangulation (Hilchot Sanhedrin 14:4), they are not made liable to the more severe death that they plotted to cause.
and they were refuted. And it became clear that they plotted to make him liable to pay her ketubah.

but whether today or tomorrow, if he divorces her he will end up paying the ketubah. It may happen sooner or later that he divorces his wife and then will have to give her the ketubah, and so it turns out that the witnesses do not cause damage equal to the entire ketubah.

we say: How much would a person be willing to pay for this woman's ketubah, etc.. That is, they assess how much a person would be willing to pay to buy a ketubah with the risk that if she dies it cannot be collected, and the witnesses must pay that same value.
and they assess the woman. What the chance is that this woman will be divorced.
and the ketubah. According to the amount of the ketubah.
for if the woman was sick or old. And there is a greater chance that she will die and the ketubah will not be collected.
or if there was peace between her and her husband. And the chance that they will divorce is smaller.

for if her ketubah was a thousand and it is sold as a possible benefit for a hundred, etc.. Since for a ketubah of large value it is worthwhile for the buyer to take the risk and pay proportionally a larger sum than he is willing to pay for a ketubah of small value.
and they were found to be conspiring. And it became clear that they wanted to make him liable to pay a debt within thirty days instead of within five years and thirty days.
we say: How much would a person be willing to pay to have a thousand zuz in his hand for five years. They assess how much postponing the date of payment by five years is worth.
they pay half damages. For the damage done by a tam ox (one not forewarned) that gored, the owner pays half the damage (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:2).

and if the ox is not worth half the damage, etc.. For the damage of a tam ox is paid only from the ox itself, and if it is worth less than half the damage its owner does not have to complete the payment from his own pocket (ibid. 1:3).
if they testified against him that it ate produce, etc.. For damage by tooth and foot the owner pays full damage (ibid. 1:2).

they testified about so-and-so that he knocked out his slave's tooth, etc.. One who strikes his Canaanite slave and knocks out his tooth or blinds his eye frees him (Hilchot Avadim 5:5). If he knocked out his tooth and afterwards blinded his eye, he frees him for the tooth and pays him the value of his eye (ibid. 5:14). Therefore when they testified to this and were found to be conspiring, they pay the master the value of the slave and, in addition, the value of his eye.

they testified that he blinded his eye and afterwards knocked out his tooth, and the matter was found to be the reverse... they pay the value of the eye to the slave. For it became clear that they plotted that the slave would receive only the small value of a tooth and lose the large value of the eye (although the value of the tooth, which the master would have had to pay in any case, is deducted from their payment - Kesef Mishneh).

witnesses of warning and seclusion who were refuted receive lashes. A woman whose husband warned her not to be secluded with a certain man ("warning") and who afterwards was secluded with him ("seclusion") is a sotah and is forbidden to her husband until she drinks the bitter waters (Hilchot Sotah 1:1-2). If witnesses came and plotted to make a woman liable as a sotah and were refuted, they are liable to lashes as conspiring witnesses who cannot be punished with what they plotted to do (above 20:9).

one witness came and testified that she committed adultery... pays her ketubah. For one witness is believed to testify that a sotah committed adultery, and she is forbidden to her husband and leaves without a ketubah (Hilchot Sotah 1:14), and so when he is found conspiring he is punished with what he plotted to make her liable.
if the witnesses of warning and seclusion and impurity were the same two. That the witnesses of the warning and seclusion also testified that she committed adultery.
they pay the equivalent of the ketubah and do not receive lashes. Because they plotted to make her lose her ketubah, and whoever pays does not receive lashes (above 18:1).
and why are they not put to death, since they testified about impurity. Surely they plotted to make her liable to death as a married woman who committed adultery.
because they did not forewarn her. And there is no death liability without forewarning, so it turns out that they did not plot to kill her.

two who testified about someone that he stole and slaughtered or sold. An ox or a sheep. One who steals an ox or sheep pays double, and if he also slaughtered or sold it he pays five times for the ox and four times for the sheep (Hilchot Genevah 1:6).
the first pay him the double payment. As they plotted to make him liable.
and the later ones pay the payments of two or three. Three for the ox and two for the sheep, for so they plotted to make him liable in addition to the double payment.

if one of the later ones is found to be conspiring, the second testimony is void. For if one of them is found disqualified, the entire testimony is void (above 5:3). However the conspiring witness does not pay, since the law of refutation applies only when all of them are refuted (above 20:1).
for if there was no theft, the slaughter or sale does not obligate him to pay anything. For it is possible that he slaughtered and sold what was his own.

two who testified that this person ate the produce of this field for three years, etc.. When a field is in one person's possession and another who was known as the owner of the field comes and claims that the field is his, if the occupant brings witnesses that he ate the field's produce for three consecutive years, it becomes his by chazakah (presumptive ownership), and he is believed to claim that he bought it or received it from the previous owners even if he brings no proof for his words (Hilchot To'ein VeNitan 11:2). When the witnesses of the chazakah are found to be conspiring, they must pay the previous owner of the field the value of the field that they wished to make him lose.
they divide it among themselves into thirds. They divide the payment among themselves so that from all of them together the amount they wanted him to lose is received.

for even though the testimony of chazakah is three testimonies, they are like one testimony for refutation. In terms of the rules of testimony these are three separate testimonies, but for refutation they are considered one testimony, as explained below.
three brothers and one who joins... and they testified, year by year. One witness testified about all three years, and for each year one of the brothers joined him.
these are three testimonies. And we do not say that they are one testimony and therefore, since it includes brothers, all of it is disqualified (Radbaz).
and they are like one testimony for refutation. Since the testimonies have no significance without one another.

the three brothers pay, etc.. They divide the payment among themselves according to their proportional share in the loss they plotted to cause him. Therefore the witness who testified about all three years pays half the value of the field, while the brothers, who each testified about one year, divide their payment among themselves and each pays one sixth of the value of the field.

that through their testimony it was established that this ox is a mu'ad (forewarned ox). Each group testified that the ox gored once, and from the sum of the testimonies it emerged that it gored three times and is a mu'ad. Now the ox gored and caused damage, and so because of their testimonies he is liable to pay full damages (and without them he would pay only half damages, like a tam ox - see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:2-4).

and the first and second groups were found to be conspiring, all of them are exempt. From paying full damages, because the three testimonies are considered one testimony for refutation, and they are liable only if all of it is refuted.
if all three were found conspiring, all of them must pay half damages. If all the testimonies that this ox gored were refuted, the witnesses must pay what they would have made the ox's owner lose.

for even though it is a tam and pays half damages. Since even for damage by a tam ox he pays the injured party half the damage, it turns out that they plotted to add to his liability only half the damage.
when they were all hinting to one another or came in succession. Together, so that it is evident that they intended to make it a mu'ad.

or they knew the owner of the ox but did not recognize the ox. In this case it is proven that they came to make it a mu'ad. For since they did not recognize which ox gored, they could not have made its owner liable for half damages (since that payment is collected only from the ox itself - see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:2), and so they came to make the owner liable for full damages, which are paid from the best of the owner's property (and this speaks of a case where they warned the owner that he has a goring ox, in which case he must guard all his cattle - see Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 24b).

but if none of these is present, the first and second groups are exempt, for they say, etc.. For they can claim that they came to testify only to make him liable for half damages for the goring they testified about, and did not intend to make it a mu'ad.

two who testified about a stubborn and rebellious son, etc.. A stubborn and rebellious son is a son who rebels against his parents, steals money from them and buys meat and wine with it, and eats and drinks them gluttonously and greedily. First his parents bring him to court, and the court gives him lashes on the basis of this testimony (the "first testimony"). If he repeats his conduct, they approach the court with witnesses that he repeated his conduct, and on the basis of this testimony (the "last testimony") the court finalizes his sentence of stoning (Hilchot Mamrim 7:1, 7:7).

because they can say, "We came to have him flogged". As is the law of a stubborn and rebellious son the first time, and they did not plot to subject him to the full law of a stubborn and rebellious son.

if the last group was four... all of them are put to death. The four witnesses of the last group are put to death, because the testimonies of the theft and the eating are needed one for the other and combine to make him liable to death, and so it turns out that all of them plotted to kill him.

two testified that this person kidnapped a Jew and sold him, and they were refuted, these are strangled. One who kidnaps a Jew, uses him and sells him is liable to death by strangulation (Hilchot Genevah 9:1-2), and they are punished with what they plotted to do.
for the kidnapping is the beginning of this one's death liability. Therefore the witnesses of the kidnapping are also liable to death, since their testimony was intended to bring about his death.
two testified that he sold him to this Israelite. They testified about so-and-so that he sold this Jewish person to another man.
because he can say, "I sold my slave". And I did not kidnap him at all.

if the witnesses of kidnapping came after the witnesses of the sale were refuted, even if we saw them hinting to one another, they are not put to death. For after the witnesses of the sale were refuted, the testimony about the kidnapping cannot bring about the defendant's death. And the hinting does not help to combine them at this stage, since the testimony of the sale is already void (see Even HaEzel).

one who defames his wife, who brought witnesses that she committed adultery while betrothed, etc.. One who defames his wife is one who falsely claimed that his wife committed adultery while betrothed, before she married him. This law applies when the husband brought witnesses that his wife committed adultery (the "husband's witnesses"), and afterwards the girl's father refuted the witnesses through other witnesses he brought (the "father's witnesses"). The husband who defames his wife is punished with lashes and a fine of one hundred silver selaim paid to the girl's father, and the witnesses he brought are liable to death by stoning, as they plotted to do to the girl (Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 3:6).

the father's witnesses are put to death and pay money to the husband, etc.. If the husband afterwards brought witnesses who refuted the father's witnesses, so that it is found that the first witnesses brought by the husband spoke the truth, then the father's witnesses plotted to put the husband's witnesses to death and also to make the husband pay a fine.

and it is found that lives are at stake for one and money for another. Although it is a rule that any transgression that carries a court-imposed death penalty has no payments (see ibid. 1:14), in this case the payment liability and the death liability are toward different people, and so they are liable to both.
who testified about someone that he had relations with a betrothed girl. And he is liable to death.
they are put to death and do not pay. Compensation to the girl's father for the decrease in the value of the girl's ketubah, since they did not say who the girl was.

he had relations with so-and-so's daughter, etc.. If they said who the girl was, they are put to death and pay the girl's father the amount of the decrease in the ketubah's value (Radbaz, and according to this the term "fine" is not exact). Some commentators explained that it is specifically a fine, for rape of a virgin girl or for defaming, and they struggled to explain why they pay the father and not the accused (see Arukh HaShulchan and others).
so-and-so had relations with the ox. The one who has relations is liable to stoning, and the ox that was the object is also sentenced to stoning (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:16).
they are stoned and do not pay. They are stoned for plotting to kill the person whom they claimed had relations, but they need not pay the value of the ox, since they did not specify a particular ox.
so-and-so's ox, etc.. When they testified about the ox of a specific person, they pay him the value of the ox they plotted to have killed.
that contradict one another. They contradict one another's words (see above 18:2).
and they testified in different testimony. They joined to testify together in another matter.
there is no testimony here, for surely one of them is a liar. And when one of the witnesses is found disqualified, the testimony of all of them is void (above 5:3).
each of them is accepted by itself. Since it is not known which of them is disqualified, each is presumed to be qualified, and neither is disqualified.
Shimon pays a maneh. For it is agreed by all that at the very least he owes him a maneh, but he does not pay more than that.
for the holder of the document has the lower hand. For surely the witnesses of one of the documents are disqualified, and money is not taken on a doubt.

by taking a sacred object. That he swears while holding a Torah scroll (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8), as in a severe oath, and not like the hesset oath, which does not require taking an object (ibid. 11:13).

for two witnesses testify against him, etc.. And just as one who admits part of the claim must take an oath by Torah law, so when witnesses testify that he is liable for part of the claim he must take an oath by Torah law.
as we have explained. Hilchot To'ein VeNitan 4:10.
for surely one of them has it with him. And since he cannot prove which group is disqualified, he may not make them lose.

and this oath is by decree of the Sages, like the law of the shopkeeper on his ledger. A householder owed money to his worker and told the shopkeeper to pay the worker on his behalf and that he would repay him afterwards. Now the shopkeeper claims that he paid the worker and the worker claims that he did not receive from him, and both sue the householder to pay them. The law is that both swear on their claims while taking a sacred object, and collect from the householder. Although by strict law they do not need to swear at all, the Sages instituted that they swear, since the householder loses from both sides collecting from him (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 16:5). So too here, by strict law they do not need to swear at all, but the Sages instituted that they swear because Levi loses from both collecting from him when he owes only one of them.
and each of them denies him. And claims that the witnesses signed on the document produced against him are the disqualified ones, and the qualified witnesses signed the other document.
they swear the hesset oath. An oath instituted by the Sages of the Talmud for one who denies the entire claim against him (Hilchot To'ein VeNitan 1:3).
when both groups came to testify as one. That Reuven produced both documents together.
for each of the two groups testified by itself. And since it is not known which of them is disqualified, each is presumed qualified, and neither is disqualified, as explained above 5:1.
and the testimony of these latter ones is found to be consistent. Precise and matching.
on whom a challenge was called out. That a rumor went out about him that he is disqualified.

even though the document was validated by its signers. That they validated the document by comparing the witnesses' signatures with their signatures on other documents, and in a validated document there is no claim of forgery.
one never collects with it. For we fear that nevertheless he managed to forge it.
